title: Getting Started with React Hooks
excerpt: Hooks let function components own state, side effects and refs without classes. Here is the mental model that makes them click.
content:
Before hooks, any component that needed state had to be a class. `useState` and `useEffect` changed that by attaching behaviour to the render itself, so a function component can own state, run side effects and keep a reference between renders.

The key mental model is that a component is just a function that runs again on every render. `useState` returns the current value plus a setter; calling the setter schedules another render with the new value. Nothing is mutated in place, everything is re-derived from props and state.

`useEffect` is where side effects live: fetching data, subscribing to a browser API, syncing a value to `localStorage`. The dependency array is the contract. An empty array means "run once after the first render", and a list of values means "re-run whenever one of these changes".

Once you internalise those two hooks, the rest (useMemo, useCallback, useRef, custom hooks) are variations on the same theme: a function that plugs into React's render cycle and cleans up after itself.

title: Building REST APIs with Express
excerpt: Routing, middleware and error handling — the three pillars of a predictable Express service.
content:
An Express application is a pipeline of middleware functions. A request enters at the top, flows through logger and body parsers, reaches the matching route handler, and either responds or calls `next(err)` to fall into the error handler at the bottom.

Keep routes thin. A route should parse the request, delegate to a service or repository, and shape the response. Business rules belong in a separate layer so they can be tested without spinning up an HTTP server.

Error handling is what separates a demo from an API. Throw a typed error with a status code from anywhere in the stack, forward it with `next(err)`, and let a single error middleware translate it into a consistent JSON payload. Clients then get the same shape whether the failure was a 404, a validation error or an unexpected crash.

Add `cors` for browser clients, `morgan` for request logs, and a health endpoint for your deploy platform. That small set of conventions gets you a long way before you need anything heavier.

title: Understanding async/await in JavaScript
excerpt: Promises with nicer syntax — plus the three pitfalls that catch almost everyone.
content:
`async/await` is syntactic sugar over promises. An `async` function always returns a promise, and `await` pauses that function until the promise settles, handing you the resolved value or throwing the rejection.

The first pitfall is sequential awaits. Writing `await a(); await b();` when the two calls are independent serialises them. Start both promises first, then await together with `Promise.all`.

The second is forgetting that `await` inside a loop is usually what you want for correctness but rarely what you want for throughput. `for...of` with `await` runs strictly in order; `Promise.all(items.map(...))` runs them concurrently with a shared failure mode.

The third is unhandled rejections. A missing `try/catch` around `await` means the error escapes to the runtime instead of your error handler. Wrap the boundary, log there, and let everything deeper throw.

Understand those three and async code stops being mysterious.

title: CSS Grid vs Flexbox: choosing the right layout tool
excerpt: Two-dimensional thinking versus one-dimensional flow. Pick the tool that matches the axis you actually have.
content:
Flexbox lays out content along a single axis. You give it a row of items, it distributes the free space, and items size themselves based on content and the `flex` shorthand. Grid lays out along two axes at once: you define tracks, and items are placed into cells.

A useful rule of thumb: if the layout is a line of things, use flexbox. If the layout is a table-like structure where rows and columns both matter, use grid.

In practice you will mix them. A page shell is a grid (`header / main / footer` rows), the card list inside `main` is a grid with `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr))`, and the toolbar inside each card is flexbox.

Modern grid also handles the awkward cases that used to need hacks: equal-height columns, sticky footers, and responsive card walls without a single media query.

title: State management in React without the ceremony
excerpt: Most apps do not need a global store. They need clear ownership of state and a couple of well-placed contexts.
content:
The first question is not "which library" but "who owns this state". State that only one component reads belongs in that component. State shared by two siblings belongs in their closest common parent. Only state that many distant branches need earns a place in a store.

React's built-in tools cover more ground than people expect. `useState` for local values, `useReducer` when transitions get complicated, `useContext` for genuinely app-wide concerns such as the current user or a theme.

Context is not a state manager. It is a transport mechanism. Pair it with `useReducer` and memoised values and you have a small, predictable store with no dependency to maintain.

Reach for an external library when you need devtools, middleware, server-state caching or time-travel debugging. Until then, colocated state and a couple of contexts keep the app easier to reason about.

title: A Node.js project structure that scales
excerpt: Group by feature, keep the edges thin, and let dependencies point in one direction.
content:
The most common failure mode in a growing Node service is a `controllers/`, `services/` and `models/` trio that balloons until every change touches all three folders. Feature folders age better: everything about posts lives under `posts/`.

Keep entry points thin. `server.js` starts the process, `app.js` composes middleware and routes, and neither contains business logic. That makes the app importable from tests without opening a port.

Let dependencies point inward. Routes may import services, services may not import routes. Data access sits behind a repository so swapping a JSON file for a database is a one-file change.

Finally, pin your conventions in the repository: scripts in `package.json`, configuration from environment variables, and a `.env.example` that documents every variable the app reads.

title: Pagination patterns for REST APIs
excerpt: Offset, cursor, and why the metadata you return matters more than the technique you pick.
content:
Offset pagination is the familiar one: `?page=2&limit=10`. It maps directly to SQL `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, it is trivially cacheable, and it is easy to render as numbered buttons. Its weakness is drift — rows inserted while a user pages through can shift items between pages.

Cursor pagination replaces the page number with an opaque marker, usually the last item's id or timestamp. It stays stable under writes and performs better deep into a dataset, at the cost of jumping straight to "page 7".

Whatever you choose, return the envelope. Alongside `data`, send `page`, `limit`, `total` and `totalPages`, plus `hasNextPage` and `hasPrevPage`. Clients should never have to infer whether another request is worth making.

Validate the inputs too. Reject a limit of `0`, cap it at something sane like 50, and fall back to defaults instead of returning a 500 when a client sends `page=abc`.

title: Debugging JavaScript like a pro
excerpt: Stop sprinkling console.log. Form a hypothesis, minimise the repro, then let the debugger answer the question.
content:
Debugging is a loop: observe, hypothesise, test, repeat. Logging is a way to observe, but it is a blunt one — you only see what you thought to print.

Start by shrinking the problem. Reproduce it in the smallest possible surface: one file, one function call, one input. Half of all bugs disappear during that step, and the rest become obvious.

The browser devtools debugger for frontend code and `node --inspect-brk` for the backend let you pause execution and inspect the real values in scope. Conditional breakpoints and watch expressions turn a slow log-and-rerun cycle into a single pass.

When the bug is timing-related, read the async boundaries first: a stale closure, a missing `await`, or an effect that runs before its dependency is ready. Nine times out of ten the culprit is a value captured from an earlier render.

title: TypeScript for React developers
excerpt: Enough types to catch real bugs — without turning your components into type puzzles.
content:
TypeScript pays for itself fastest at the boundaries: props, API responses and event handlers. Type those and the compiler starts finding mistakes for free.

For props, a plain `type Props = { ... }` is enough. Avoid over-abstracting with generics until you actually need to reuse a component across shapes.

For API data, describe the response envelope once and reuse it everywhere. A `Post` interface plus a `Paginated<T>` wrapper gives you autocomplete in the UI layer and a single place to update when the contract changes.

Use discriminated unions for loading states: `{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success', data: T } | { status: 'error', error: string }`. The compiler then guarantees you cannot read `data` before checking the status — the exact class of bug that makes UI code fragile.

Turn on `strict` from day one. Retrofitting it later is far more painful than writing against it from the start.

title: Optimising for Core Web Vitals
excerpt: LCP, INP and CLS explained in terms of the decisions you actually control.
content:
Largest Contentful Paint measures when the biggest element in the viewport finishes painting. Most of the time it is your hero image or a web font, so the fixes are concrete: serve modern formats, set explicit dimensions, preload the one image that matters.

Interaction to Next Paint replaced the old first-input metric. It rewards keeping long tasks short — break up heavy work, defer non-critical JavaScript, and avoid re-rendering an entire tree to update one row.

Cumulative Layout Shift punishes content that moves after it renders. Reserve space for images and embeds, avoid injecting banners above existing content, and prefer `font-display: swap` with a metric-compatible fallback font.

Measure on real devices with real network conditions. A score from a fast laptop on wifi tells you very little about the users who will actually judge your site.

title: Testing React apps with Vitest
excerpt: A practical test pyramid for components: behaviour first, implementation rarely.
content:
The goal of a component test is to describe behaviour a user would recognise: renders the loading state, shows an error when the request fails, moves to the next page when the button is clicked.

Vitest plus React Testing Library gives you exactly that vocabulary. `render`, `screen.findByRole`, `userEvent.click` — all of it queries the DOM the way a user perceives it, which is why the tests survive refactors.

Mock at the network boundary, not the module boundary. Stub `fetch` or your API client and let the real components, hooks and reducers run. You get integration coverage without a running server.

Keep the pyramid in mind. A handful of end-to-end smoke tests, a solid band of integration tests, and unit tests for pure logic such as pagination maths and formatters. That mix finds bugs quickly and does not slow your pipeline to a crawl.

title: From junior to senior: the skills nobody assigns you
excerpt: Writing code is the entry ticket. Judgement, communication and scope are the career.
content:
Junior engineers are measured on tasks completed. Senior engineers are measured on problems removed. The shift happens when you stop waiting for a ticket to be perfectly specified and start clarifying the goal behind it.

Communication compounds faster than any framework skill. Writing a short, clear proposal before building, and a short, clear summary after shipping, makes your work visible and reviews painless.

Learn to estimate in ranges and to say "I don't know yet, here is how I would find out". Both are more valuable than false confidence, and both build the trust that gets you bigger scope.

Finally, invest in debugging and reading unfamiliar code. Every new language and framework becomes cheap once you can navigate a codebase you have never seen and find the line that is lying to you.

title: useEffect cleanup functions, explained properly
excerpt: Every effect that starts something should be able to stop it. The cleanup is not optional polish.
content:
An effect that subscribes, starts a timer or opens a connection owns a resource. If the component unmounts without releasing it, you leak. The cleanup function returned from `useEffect` is where that release happens.

The rule that surprises people is that React also runs the cleanup before re-running the effect on the next dependency change. That is deliberate: it guarantees the effect always sees a consistent world instead of layering a second subscription on top of the first.

A timer example makes it concrete. Start `setInterval` inside the effect, return `clearInterval`. Skip the return and you have two intervals after the dependency changes once, three after it changes twice.

For data fetching the cleanup is usually an `AbortController`. Abort the request in the return function and the effect ignores the result if the component has already moved on — which is exactly the fix for the classic setState-after-unmount warning.

title: Node.js streams without the fear
excerpt: Readable, writable, transform, pipeline — four names that cover almost every streaming task you will meet.
content:
A stream is a sequence of data delivered in chunks instead of all at once. That single property is why you can process a 2 GB file on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM: you never hold the whole thing.

A readable produces data, a writable consumes it, and a transform sits in the middle changing each chunk as it passes. `pipe` wires them together, but `pipeline` from `stream/promises` is the modern choice because it propagates errors and destroys every stream in the chain when one fails.

Backpressure is the concept worth internalising. When a writable cannot keep up, it signals the readable to slow down rather than buffering without limit. Ignore it and a fast producer plus a slow consumer becomes an out-of-memory crash.

For JSON APIs the common pattern is a line-delimited export: read a cursor, write each record with `JSON.stringify` plus a newline, and let the client parse the stream. The memory profile stays flat no matter how large the dataset grows.

title: The JavaScript array methods you actually need
excerpt: map, filter, reduce and find cover the vast majority of loops you write. The rest are details.
content:
A `for` loop that builds one array from another is almost always a `map`. A loop that builds an array conditionally is a `filter`. Learning to see those two patterns removes a surprising number of lines from a codebase.

`reduce` is the one people avoid, and it earns a bad reputation mostly from being used where `map` or `filter` would be clearer. Where it shines is genuine accumulation: summing totals, grouping by a key, building a lookup object in a single pass.

`find` and `some` short-circuit, which means they stop as soon as they have an answer. That distinction matters on large arrays where a `filter` plus `[0]` would scan everything.

One caution: `sort` mutates. In a React render path or a Redux reducer that mutation is a bug. Copy first with the spread operator, then sort the copy.

title: CSS custom properties in practice
excerpt: Variables that live in the cascade, not in a preprocessor. That difference unlocks theming for free.
content:
Unlike Sass variables, custom properties are resolved at runtime by the browser. They participate in the cascade and in inheritance, which is what makes theming possible without rebuilding a stylesheet.

Define your tokens once on `:root` — colours, spacing steps, radii, font sizes — then read them everywhere with `var(--token)`. A design change becomes a one-line edit rather than a search and replace.

Because they inherit, a component can override a token for its own subtree and every descendant picks it up. A dark section sets `--surface` and every card inside flips without any of them knowing about dark mode.

They also work in places preprocessor variables cannot: inline styles set from JavaScript, media queries driven by a single value, and fallbacks with `var(--token, red)` for progressive enhancement.

title: Designing idempotent APIs
excerpt: Retries are inevitable. Idempotency keys are how you make them safe.
content:
Networks fail in the worst possible window: after the server has done the work but before the client hears about it. The client retries, and without protection the work happens twice.

HTTP already gives you idempotency for free on GET, PUT and DELETE — repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. The problem is POST, which creates something new every time.

The standard fix is an idempotency key. The client sends a unique header per logical operation, the server records the key with its result, and any repeat with the same key returns the stored response instead of performing the action again.

Combine that with a sensible retention window and a conflict response when the same key arrives with a different body, and your create endpoints survive flaky mobile networks and over-eager retry middleware alike.

title: TypeScript generics in practice
excerpt: Generics are for relationships between types, not for showing off. Start with the simplest signature that works.
content:
A generic is a way to say "this type varies, but the variation is consistent". `function first<T>(items: T[]): T` promises that whatever you put in comes back out with the same type — lose the generic and you are back to `any`.

The moment they pay off is when two positions must agree. A `useApi` hook that returns the same shape the fetcher produced, a repository that returns the model it was constructed with, an event emitter where the listener argument matches the emitter's payload.

Constraints are where generics stop being magic. `T extends { id: string }` lets the body use `id` safely while still preserving the caller's concrete type.

Avoid the trap of adding type parameters a function does not need. If one call site uses the generic, it is a parameter; if it is never inferred from an argument, it is probably just a concrete type wearing a costume.

title: Lazy loading routes in React
excerpt: Split by route, not by atom. The first paint is what users judge you on.
content:
A single JavaScript bundle means a user downloading your admin dashboard before they can read the homepage. Route-level code splitting is the cheapest, highest-impact fix available.

`React.lazy` plus `Suspense` turns a component into a dynamically imported chunk. Wrap the routes in a `Suspense` boundary with a fallback that matches your layout so the wait does not shift content around.

In a Vite or webpack build the bundler then emits one chunk per route, and the browser only fetches the chunk for the page it is actually rendering. A visitor landing on the blog list never downloads the editor.

The next step, when a single route is still heavy, is to split below the route — defer a charting library or a markdown renderer until the component that needs it mounts. Measure with the network panel before deciding.

title: Rate limiting your API without breaking clients
excerpt: Protect the service, tell clients the rules, and make the limits observable.
content:
Rate limiting exists to stop a single caller starving everyone else, whether through a bug, a scraped endpoint or a deliberate flood. The mechanism matters less than the contract around it.

The simplest useful algorithm is a fixed window counter: allow N requests per key per minute. It is easy to implement in memory for a single instance and cheap to reason about, with the known weakness that a caller can burst across a window boundary.

A sliding window or token bucket smooths that out at the cost of a little bookkeeping. Behind multiple instances you need shared state — Redis with an atomic increment and expiry is the usual answer.

What clients need is predictability: a `429` status, a `Retry-After` header, and ideally `RateLimit-Limit` and `RateLimit-Remaining` so well-behaved consumers can back off before they are blocked. A limit no one can see is just an outage waiting to be reported.

title: Environment variables done right
excerpt: Config that comes from the environment, is validated at boot, and never lands in git.
content:
The twelve-factor rule is simple: configuration that varies between deploys lives in the environment, not in the code. Everything a developer would want to change without a rebuild qualifies.

Read them once, in one place, at startup. Scattering `process.env.X` through the codebase means you discover a missing variable only when that branch executes — usually in production.

Validate at boot instead. A tiny schema check that asserts `PORT` is a number and `DATABASE_URL` exists will fail the process immediately on a bad deploy rather than half an hour later on the first request that needs it.

Document every variable in a `.env.example` that is committed, keep the real `.env` ignored, and give the values defaults where defaults make sense. A new developer should be able to clone, copy the example, and run without reading the source.

title: Writing good commit messages
excerpt: A commit message is a letter to a stranger — usually yourself, six months from now.
content:
The diff already says what changed. The message should say why. That distinction is what makes a history useful when you are hunting for the commit that introduced a behaviour.

The conventional shape is a short imperative subject under about fifty characters, a blank line, then a body that explains the motivation and any trade-off you accepted. "Fix bug" tells a reader nothing; "Handle empty page query without a 500" tells them everything they need.

Imperative mood — "add", "fix", "remove" — reads naturally in the generated summaries that tools produce, and it keeps the subject consistent across a team.

Commit in coherent units. One logical change per commit makes `git bisect`, revert and review all easier, and it is the single habit that most improves the quality of everything downstream.

title: SQL indexes for beginners
excerpt: An index trades write speed and disk for read speed. Knowing when that trade is worth it is the whole skill.
content:
A query without a usable index scans every row. On a table with ten thousand rows that is invisible; on ten million it is the difference between a request and a timeout.

An index is a sorted structure the database maintains alongside the data. Because it is sorted, a lookup on the indexed column can jump straight to the matching range instead of reading everything.

The cost is real. Every insert, update and delete has to update every index that covers the changed columns, and each index occupies disk. Indexing every column is a classic over-correction that makes writes slow and changes nothing about read performance.

Order matters in composite indexes: an index on `(user_id, created_at)` serves queries filtered by user, or by user and date, but not by date alone. Put the equality column first and the range column second, then check the query plan to confirm the index is actually being used.

title: Caching strategies for web apps
excerpt: Cache in the right layer, invalidate on purpose, and never trust a cache you cannot clear.
content:
Caching is the highest-leverage performance work available, and also the fastest way to serve stale, confusing data. The two facts are inseparable.

Start at the HTTP layer. `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` on an API response lets browsers and CDNs do the work for you. Fingerprinted asset filenames can be cached for a year with `immutable` because the name changes whenever the content does.

Inside the application, cache the expensive, rarely changing lookups — a category list, a config document — with an explicit time to live. A cache without expiry is a permanent bug in waiting.

Invalidation is the design decision, not an afterthought. Prefer cache keys that become invalid naturally, such as a version suffix, over logic that has to hunt down and delete entries. If you cannot name exactly when an entry should die, you are not ready to cache it.

title: Accessible forms from the start
excerpt: Labels, error messages and focus order. Getting them right early is far cheaper than retrofitting.
content:
Every input needs a programmatically associated label. An `<label for="email">` tied to the input's id does it, and it also enlarges the click target. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears the moment the user types.

Errors belong next to the field and in the accessibility tree. Render the message, link it to the input with `aria-describedby`, and set `aria-invalid` so a screen reader announces the state instead of leaving the user to guess.

Do not rely on colour alone. Red text without an icon or a word is invisible to a chunk of your audience. Say what went wrong in plain language: "Enter an email address in the format name@example.com".

Finally, respect focus order and never remove the focus ring. Keyboard users navigate by tab, and a visible outline is the only thing telling them where they are. Group related fields in a `fieldset` with a `legend` and the whole form becomes navigable rather than guessable.

title: Error boundaries in React
excerpt: One thrown component should not white-screen the whole application.
content:
React unmounts the entire tree when a render throws. Without a boundary, a single bad prop in one card takes down the page around it.

An error boundary is a component that catches errors from its children during rendering, in lifecycle methods and in constructors, then renders a fallback instead. It still has to be a class component, which is why this is one of the few places `componentDidCatch` survives in a hooks codebase.

Place boundaries at meaningful seams rather than one at the root. Around each route, and around any independently failing widget, so the rest of the page stays usable while the failure is contained.

Boundaries do not catch errors from event handlers or from asynchronous code. Those come from `try/catch` and from a rejected promise. The division of labour is worth remembering: boundaries handle render-time surprises, your own error handling covers everything else.

title: npm scripts that earn their keep
excerpt: A tiny set of memorable commands beats a wiki page nobody reads.
content:
Scripts in `package.json` are the documented entry points to a project. If a new contributor has to ask how to start the dev server, the scripts are wrong.

Cover the essentials: `dev`, `build`, `start`, `test`, and `lint`. Keep the names consistent across repositories so muscle memory transfers and nobody is guessing between `serve`, `run` and `dev-server`.

Compose rather than duplicate. A `lint:fix` that calls the linter with `--fix`, a `test:watch` that reuses the test runner with a flag, a `ci` that chains lint, test and build so local and pipeline run the same steps.

Use `pre` and `post` hooks sparingly. A `pretest` that quietly migrates a database is a surprising side effect. Explicit chains — `npm run build && npm test` — are easier to debug when something in the middle fails.

title: Connecting React to a REST API
excerpt: One fetch wrapper, one hook, and a clear separation between transport and presentation.
content:
Keep the network in one module. A small `client.js` that owns the base URL, sets headers and turns every failure into a consistent error object means components never deal with raw `Response` objects.

Wrap that client in a hook. A `useApi` that returns a status, data and an error removes the boilerplate of loading flags and cancelled requests from every screen, and makes the behaviour identical wherever it is used.

Represent state as a status instead of two booleans. `loading` plus `error` plus `data` admits impossible combinations such as both loading and errored. A single discriminated status cannot.

Always cancel in-flight work on unmount with an `AbortController`, and ignore the abort in the catch block. That one detail eliminates the flaky warnings and race conditions that make API-connected UIs feel unpredictable.

title: Avoiding prop drilling without a store
excerpt: Composition and context solve most of it. Reach for a state library last.
content:
Prop drilling is passing a value through five components that do not use it, purely so the sixth can. It makes every intermediate layer depend on something it has no business knowing about.

The first fix is composition. Instead of passing data down so a child can render it, pass the rendered element down as `children`. The intermediate components stop needing the data at all.

The second is context, for values with a genuinely wide reach: the current user, the theme, a locale. Extract the provider and a `useX` consumer hook into the same module so the context object never leaks and consumers fail loudly when the provider is missing.

Split contexts by change frequency. A context holding both a rarely changing user and a rapidly changing counter re-renders every consumer on every tick. Two contexts, two re-render scopes.

title: Understanding the JavaScript event loop
excerpt: One thread, a task queue and a microtask queue. Everything async follows from that.
content:
JavaScript runs your code on a single thread with one call stack. Asynchronous behaviour comes from the host environment — the browser or Node — scheduling work and handing results back when the stack is empty.

The loop takes a task from the macrotask queue, runs it to completion, then drains the entire microtask queue before taking the next task. Promise callbacks and `queueMicrotask` are microtasks; timers and I/O callbacks are macrotasks.

That ordering explains behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary. A resolved promise callback always runs before a `setTimeout(..., 0)`, no matter which was written first, because the microtask queue is drained first.

It also explains why a long synchronous loop freezes the UI: nothing else can run until the stack clears. Chunking heavy work, or moving it to a worker, is the only real remedy.

title: Docker for Node developers
excerpt: A Dockerfile that builds fast, runs small, and does not ship your node_modules.
content:
The goal of a container image is a reproducible runtime, not a copy of your laptop. Start from a slim base, copy `package.json` and the lockfile first, install, then copy the source. Layer caching then means an edit to a source file does not reinstall dependencies.

Build for production with `npm ci --omit=dev`. The lockfile guarantees the exact tree that passed CI, and skipping dev dependencies keeps the runtime image free of test runners and bundlers.

Run as a non-root user. Creating a user and switching with `USER` costs one line and closes an escalation path that container escape exploits rely on.

Finally, write a `.dockerignore` that excludes `node_modules`, `.git` and local environment files. Without it the build context bloats and you risk baking secrets into a layer that lives in the registry forever.

title: REST vs GraphQL: an honest comparison
excerpt: Neither wins outright. The shape of your data and your clients decides.
content:
REST organises the API around resources and HTTP semantics. It is cacheable by default, easy to explore in a browser, and every tool in the ecosystem understands it. Its weakness is over-fetching: a mobile client often needs a fraction of what an endpoint returns.

GraphQL lets the client declare exactly the fields it wants in a single request, which is genuinely valuable when many screens share a graph of related data. The cost is a query language to learn, resolvers to maintain, and access control that has to be enforced per field rather than per route.

HTTP caching is the decisive practical difference. A REST GET response slots into CDNs and browser caches for free; GraphQL typically posts to a single endpoint and needs application-level caching to get the same benefit.

The honest recommendation for most teams is REST until a client actually suffers. Firm up the resource design, add field selection where it hurts, and revisit GraphQL when the number of bespoke endpoints starts to feel like a symptom rather than a solution.

title: Debouncing and throttling
excerpt: One waits for quiet, the other paces the calls. Using the wrong one is a bug you can feel.
content:
Debouncing delays execution until the calls stop. Type in a search box and you want one request after the user pauses, not one per keystroke. That is debounce.

Throttling caps how often a function may run. Scroll and resize handlers fire dozens of times a second; a throttle that lets the handler run every hundred milliseconds keeps the UI responsive without doing needless work.

Implement both with a timer rather than a counter. A debounce resets the timer on every call; a throttle starts a timer that ignores calls while it is pending. Retain the latest arguments so the trailing call uses fresh values.

Remember the cleanup. A debounced handler that outlives its component will call a stale setter. Return a cancel function and invoke it in the effect cleanup so pending timers never fire after unmount.

title: Responsive design without media queries
excerpt: Intrinsic layout lets components adapt to their container instead of the viewport.
content:
Media queries ask about the viewport, but components care about their own space. A card in a sidebar and the same card in the main column hit the same breakpoint at very different widths.

Container queries fix that directly: declare `container-type: inline-size` on the parent, then write rules that respond to the container's size. The component becomes genuinely reusable because it adapts to wherever you place it.

Fluid sizing removes the rest of the breakpoints. `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)` scales a heading smoothly between a floor and a ceiling with no steps and no jumps.

Add `minmax` with `auto-fit` for grids that reflow on their own — `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))` gives you a card wall that goes from four columns to one and never needs a media query to do it.

title: Testing API endpoints with Supertest
excerpt: Exercise the real HTTP stack in-process, with no port and no flakiness.
content:
Supertest takes your Express app — the exported module, not a running server — and fires requests at it in memory. No port binding, no startup timing, no port collisions in CI.

The pattern that keeps tests fast is to import `app` from a module that composes middleware and routes but never calls `listen`. That separation between composing an app and running it is worth designing for from the first commit.

Assert on the contract, not the implementation. Check the status code, the shape of the envelope, and that a missing post returns a 404 with your standard error body. Those are the promises clients depend on.

Cover the edges too: invalid query parameters should be a 400, an out-of-range page a 404, a normal request a 200 with the expected count. A dozen such tests catch the regressions that break clients without breaking your own UI.

title: Refactoring legacy code safely
excerpt: Pin the behaviour with tests, change one axis at a time, and never mix a refactor with a feature.
content:
The first move in unfamiliar code is not to improve it, it is to understand it. Write a test that captures what it currently does — even the parts that look wrong — so you have a safety net before you touch anything.

Then change one thing per commit. Renaming, extracting a function and altering a branch in a single diff makes the review impossible and the rollback all-or-nothing. Small, reversible steps let you stop anywhere.

Separate refactoring from behaviour change completely. A refactor should leave every test green without edits; if a test needs updating, you changed behaviour and that deserves its own commit and its own justification.

The end state is not the point. Refactoring is continuous — you improve the areas you must touch for the current task and leave the rest, rather than planning a rewrite that never ships.

title: Handling file uploads in Express
excerpt: Multipart parsing, size limits, and treating every filename as hostile.
content:
Uploads arrive as `multipart/form-data`, which the built-in JSON parser ignores. A middleware such as `multer` parses the stream and exposes the files alongside the text fields.

Set a size limit explicitly. Without one, a single request can fill the disk or exhaust memory, and the failure arrives as an outage rather than a validation message. Reject oversized files with a 413 and a clear body.

Validate the type by content, not by the extension the client supplied. The `Content-Type` header and the filename are both attacker-controlled. Check magic bytes or re-encode the image before storing it.

Finally, never trust the filename. Generate your own identifier, store files outside the web root, and serve them through a route that checks authorisation. A path built from user input is a directory traversal vulnerability in waiting.

title: Server state is not client state
excerpt: Caching, refetching and staleness are a different problem from component state. Treat them separately.
content:
Copying fetched data into component state is the root of a family of bugs: stale copies, duplicated requests and manual refetches scattered through effects.

Server state has properties client state does not: it lives elsewhere, it can go stale without you knowing, and it is shared between screens. Caching libraries like React Query model those properties directly.

They give you a cache keyed by query, deduplication of simultaneous requests, background refetching on focus, and explicit invalidation after a mutation. All the plumbing you would otherwise hand-roll badly.

Even if you never adopt a library, adopt the mental model. Keep the cache as the single source of truth for remote data, derive what you render from it, and let mutations invalidate rather than patch.

title: A pragmatic web accessibility checklist
excerpt: Semantics, keyboard, contrast, labels. Four areas that cover most real-world failures.
content:
Start with semantics. Use `button` for actions, `a` for navigation, and headings in order. Screen readers build their navigation model from these, and no amount of ARIA rescues a `div` pretending to be a control.

Then keyboard. Every interactive element must be reachable by tab and operable by enter or space, with a visible focus indicator. Trap focus only inside genuine modals, and always return it to the trigger on close.

Contrast is measurable: a 4.5 to 1 ratio for body text, 3 to 1 for large text, using a checker rather than your eye. This one test surfaces issues that affect far more users than any single assistive technology.

Finally, labels and alternates. Every input gets a label, every image gets meaningful alt text or an empty one if purely decorative, and every error is announced. Audit with the keyboard alone — it is the fastest reality check available.

title: Designing a design system that survives
excerpt: Tokens, primitives, patterns. Ship the smallest layer that removes duplication.
content:
A design system is not a component library. It is a shared language — tokens for colour, spacing and type, plus the components built from them — owned jointly by design and engineering.

Start with tokens because they are the change that propagates. A spacing scale and a colour palette expressed as CSS custom properties let a rebrand touch one file instead of hundreds of rules.

Then build primitives: Button, Input, Card. Resist the urge to encode every product-specific layout into the system. A component with eleven boolean props for eleven one-off screens is a design problem wearing a component costume.

Version it and document it. The components need to be installable, changelogged and previewable in isolation, or teams will quietly fork them and the system becomes an archaeology project.

title: Monitoring Node apps in production
excerpt: Logs, metrics and traces for a service you cannot attach a debugger to.
content:
In production you cannot pause and inspect. You have three signals instead: structured logs for what happened, metrics for how the system behaves over time, and traces for where a request spent its time.

Log in JSON. A message interpolated into a string is unqueryable, whereas `{"level":"error","route":"/api/posts","status":500}` lets you ask real questions later. Include a request id on every line so a single user journey can be reconstructed.

Watch a small set of metrics closely: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles and event loop lag. Averages hide the problem; the ninety-fifth percentile is what users actually experience.

Add health and readiness endpoints, and alert on symptoms rather than causes. The question to encode is not "is CPU high" but "are users failing to get responses", and page a human only when the answer is yes.

title: JWT authentication explained without the myths
excerpt: What a token actually proves, and the storage decision that matters far more than the algorithm.
content:
A JSON Web Token is a signed claim, not an encrypted one. Anyone holding it can read the payload — signatures prove integrity and origin, they do not keep secrets. Never put anything sensitive inside.

The auth flow is straightforward: the client exchanges credentials for a token, sends it on subsequent requests in an `Authorization: Bearer` header, and the server verifies the signature without a database lookup. That statelessness is the appeal and also the problem, because revocation means a blocklist or short lifetimes.

The storage question is the one that causes real incidents. `localStorage` is readable by any script and therefore exposed to cross-site scripting. An `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, at the cost of needing CSRF protection.

The pragmatic answer for most apps is a short-lived access token plus a longer-lived refresh token, with the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie and rotation on every use. Combine that with https everywhere and it is a defensible baseline.

title: Modern CSS selectors worth knowing
excerpt: is, where, has and nth-child with an of clause. Less markup, fewer classes.
content:
`:is()` lets you group a selector list without repeating the whole thing: `:is(h1, h2, h3) + p` styles paragraphs after any heading level. It also forgives invalid selectors in the list, so a vendor-specific selector cannot kill the whole rule.

`:where()` behaves the same but contributes zero specificity. That makes it perfect for resets and defaults, because any later rule overrides it without needing a fight or an `!important`.

`:has()` finally lets a parent react to its children — `.card:has(img)` styles only cards containing an image. Layouts that needed a JavaScript class toggle are now a selector.

`nth-child(An+B of S)` adds a filter, so `li:nth-child(odd of .visible)` counts only visible items. Together these collapse whole categories of JavaScript into the stylesheet, where they belong.

title: Reducing your JavaScript bundle size
excerpt: Measure first, then split, tree-shake and defer. Guessing is how you waste a sprint.
content:
Open the bundle analyser before changing anything. A treemap almost always contains a surprise: a date library importing every locale, a UI kit pulled in for one component, a polyfill you no longer need.

The cheapest wins are imports. Importing a single function from a large library sometimes drags in the whole package unless it is tree-shakeable. Check the module fields, and prefer packages marketed as ESM with side-effect-free exports.

Then split. Route-level chunks mean the login page does not ship the dashboard, and a dynamic `import()` inside an event handler defers a heavy editor until the user opens it.

Finally, defer what is not needed for first paint. Load analytics and chat widgets after the page is interactive, and set the right `loading` and `fetchpriority` hints on images. Every kilobyte you move off the critical path is a faster interaction.

title: Writing documentation developers actually read
excerpt: Lead with the task, show a working example, and keep it beside the code.
content:
Documentation fails when it is organised around the system rather than the reader's goal. Someone arriving at your API docs wants to make one call succeed, not read a taxonomy of concepts.

Lead with a runnable example. A curl command and its response, or a five-line snippet that works when pasted, teaches more in ten seconds than three paragraphs of prose. Put it first, and keep the reference material below it.

The best documentation lives in the repository. A README that explains how to install, run and test, doc comments on the non-obvious functions, and a short architecture note for anything surprising. Anything further away drifts out of date within a release or two.

Treat stale docs as bugs. If a change makes a sentence untrue, updating that sentence belongs in the same pull request as the change.

title: Immutability in JavaScript, practically
excerpt: Copy the path you change, leave the rest alone, and let reference equality do the work.
content:
Mutating an object that another part of the program holds a reference to is how you get bugs that cannot be reproduced. The fix is not to freeze everything, it is to update by producing a new value.

The idiom is to copy the path from the root to the change and share everything else. Adding a post to a list is `[...posts, post]`; updating one item is `posts.map(p => p.id === id ? { ...p, title } : p)`. Untouched items keep their identity, which is exactly what memoisation needs.

Spread syntax is shallow, so nesting matters. For a deep update you reproduce each level along the path; everything off the path is reused by reference, which keeps the copy cheap.

With this discipline, `React.memo` and dependency arrays work as intended, because a value that did not change compares equal by reference. Immutability is not a style preference; it is what makes referential checks meaningful.

title: Building a CLI with Node.js
excerpt: Argument parsing, helpful output and a sane exit code. The details that make a tool pleasant.
content:
A CLI is an interface, and the same rules apply as to a UI. Discovery matters: `--help` should list the commands and options without requiring documentation, and every error message should say what to do next.

Parse arguments with a library rather than by hand. It handles short and long flags, `--key=value` and `--key value`, defaults, and the generated usage text you would otherwise forget to write.

Write to the right streams. Normal output goes to stdout so it can be piped; progress, warnings and errors go to stderr so they do not corrupt that output. This is the difference between a tool that composes and one that does not.

Exit deliberately. `process.exitCode = 1` on failure lets pending writes flush, and a nonzero code is what makes the tool usable in a shell script or a CI step. A command that fails silently with exit code zero is worse than one that crashes.

title: Form validation patterns in React
excerpt: Validate on blur and on submit, not on every keystroke. Users hate being wrong while typing.
content:
The timing of validation is a user-experience decision, not an implementation detail. Validating on every keystroke tells a person their email is invalid while they are halfway through typing it.

A workable default: validate a field on blur the first time, then live once it has been touched. Already-validated fields give immediate feedback; untouched ones stay quiet.

Keep the validation rules as pure functions so they can be tested and reused. A schema per form — required, format, cross-field dependencies such as password confirmation — beats imperative checks scattered through handlers.

On submit, focus the first invalid field and move focus there. It is a small touch that saves keyboard users an entire tab-through, and it is the kind of detail that separates a form that works from one that feels considered.

title: Mocking in tests without regret
excerpt: Mock at the boundary you do not own, and keep the rest real.
content:
Every mock is a promise about how something behaves. When the real thing changes and the mock does not, tests stay green while production breaks. That is the cost to manage, not to ignore.

The safest place to mock is a boundary you do not control: the network, the clock, a payment provider. Those are the interactions that are slow, costly or non-deterministic, and the ones worth replacing.

Avoid mocking your own modules. If a test stubs an internal function, it asserts on implementation rather than behaviour and breaks on every refactor. Inject the dependency instead, and pass a fake at the edge.

Prefer fakes to assertions about calls. A small in-memory implementation of a repository is easier to read than a chain of expectations, and it exercises more of your real code. Assert on the outcome the user would see.

title: Semantic HTML still matters
excerpt: The right element is faster than the right framework setting, and it comes with accessibility built in.
content:
Choosing `button` over a clickable `div` gets you keyboard activation, focus handling and the correct role in the accessibility tree for free. Reimplementing all three in JavaScript is a chore you opted into.

Landmarks do the same at page scale. `header`, `nav`, `main`, `footer` and `aside` give assistive technology a map, and give you a layout structure that reads clearly without any class names.

Headings are the table of contents. One `h1` per page and a nesting order without gaps lets both people and crawlers skim. Skipping from `h1` to `h4` for visual size is what CSS is for.

Do not reach for ARIA first. The rule of thumb is that the best ARIA is no ARIA, because native elements are already tested against every browser and screen reader combination. Use the attribute only when no element expresses the semantics you need.

title: Optimistic UI updates, done carefully
excerpt: Show the result before the server confirms it, then reconcile honestly when it fails.
content:
Waiting several hundred milliseconds for a round trip after a click makes an app feel slow even when it is not. An optimistic update applies the change immediately and treats the server response as confirmation.

The first rule is to keep the previous value. If the request fails you must roll back to the exact prior state, not to a guess, or the UI ends up showing something that never existed.

The second rule is to make the failure visible. A silent revert looks like the app ignored the click. Roll back, surface a message, and offer a retry.

The third is to handle out-of-order responses. If two updates target the same item, applying them in arrival order can produce the wrong final state. Attach a sequence or timestamp and discard stale responses rather than trusting whichever finishes last.

title: Database migrations without fear
excerpt: Forward-only, one change per file, and never assume the old code is gone.
content:
A migration is a version control commit for your schema. Keeping them in the repository, numbered and applied in order, means any environment can be rebuilt from nothing and any change can be traced to a deployment.

The hard part is that old and new code run simultaneously during a rolling deploy. Dropping a column the moment the schema changes breaks every instance still running the previous release.

The pattern that avoids this is expand and contract. Add the new column, deploy code that writes to both, backfill, switch reads over, stop writing to the old column, and only then drop it — four deploys instead of one, and zero downtime.

Keep each migration small and reversible where practical, and test the migration against a copy of production data. A migration that takes a long lock on a large table is an outage, not a deploy.

title: Logging best practices for backend services
excerpt: Log events, not narration. Include context, pick levels deliberately, and never log secrets.
content:
A log line should describe an event that happened, with enough context to act on it. "Processing request" tells you nothing; "order payment failed" with an order id, a provider and a reason tells you where to look.

Choose levels by what a human should do. `error` means someone should investigate, `warn` means something unexpected but handled, `info` records a meaningful state change, `debug` is for development only. Logging everything at `info` is how alerts get ignored.

Always include a correlation id so a request can be followed across services and interleaved log lines can be reassembled into a story.

And keep credentials out. Passwords, tokens and full card numbers must never reach a log file, because logs are copied, shipped and retained far more casually than a database. Redact at the point of logging, not by hoping.

title: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events
excerpt: One is bidirectional, one is a stream. Most real-time features only need the stream.
content:
Server-Sent Events is a plain HTTP response that stays open and pushes text frames to the browser. It reconnects automatically, it flows through proxies and CDNs, and the client API is a few lines. For a feed, a notification badge or a progress stream it is the right tool.

WebSockets give you a full duplex channel. That matters for chat, collaborative editing and anything where the client sends as often as it receives. The price is a separate protocol, your own reconnection and heartbeat logic, and more infrastructure to keep the connections alive.

A useful default is to reach for SSE until you can name the feature that requires the client to push. Plenty of products ship a WebSocket layer and use it in one direction only.

Either way, design for disconnection. Connections drop, tabs sleep, and phones switch networks. Make the client able to resume from the last event it processed, and the feature survives the real world.

title: Code review etiquette that speeds teams up
excerpt: Review the code, ask real questions, and make small pull requests a habit.
content:
A review is a conversation about a change, not a verdict on a person. Framing comments as questions — "what happens here if the list is empty?" — gets a better outcome than a command, and costs nothing.

Keep pull requests small. A review of fifty lines gets read carefully; a review of a thousand gets skimmed and approved. If a change is large, split it into a sequence that is each independently reviewable.

Separate blocking issues from suggestions and say which is which. Not every preference needs to be addressed, and muddying the two trains people to ignore feedback altogether.

The reviewer's job is to catch correctness, security and maintainability problems, not to rewrite the change in their own style. Approve when it is better than what is there and correct, even if it is not exactly how you would have written it.

title: Git rebase vs merge
excerpt: Merge preserves history, rebase rewrites it. Pick a policy and apply it consistently.
content:
A merge commit records that two lines of development joined. Nothing is rewritten, the topology is truthful, and the cost is a history that can look like a subway map.

Rebase replays your commits on top of a new base, producing a linear history as though you had started from the latest main. The result is easier to read and easier to bisect, but it rewrites commit hashes, so it must never be applied to commits anyone else has pulled.

A workable convention is to rebase your own feature branch onto main to stay current, then merge it in with a merge commit or a squash so the mainline records one intentional entry per change.

Interactive rebase is the real prize: squash fix-up commits, reorder for clarity, and fix a message before anyone sees it. Cleaning up before review is a courtesy to every future reader of the log.

title: Feature flags in practice
excerpt: Ship behind a switch, roll out gradually, and delete the flag when it is done.
content:
A feature flag decouples deployment from release. Code can be merged and deployed while the behaviour stays off, which turns a risky big-bang release into a gradual rollout you can stop.

The flags that earn their keep are short-lived and specific: a release toggle for a new screen, an experiment toggle for a variant, an operational toggle for a risky dependency. Give each one an owner and an intended removal date.

Evaluate flags on the server where you can. It keeps the decision in one place, prevents stale client caches from showing the wrong branch, and makes the rollout measurable.

The failure mode is accumulation. A codebase with two hundred permanent flags is unmaintainable, and every stale flag is a branch nobody dares delete. Removing the flag as part of the same work that finishes the rollout is the discipline that keeps the practice healthy.

title: Image optimisation for the web
excerpt: Right format, right size, explicit dimensions. Most page weight lives in the images.
content: Images are usually the largest part of a page, which makes them the largest opportunity. The first decision is format: WebP or AVIF for photographs, SVG for icons and logos, and JPEG only as a legacy fallback. Serve the size you need. A 3000-pixel hero rendered at 800 is wasted bytes and wasted decode time. Generate a few widths, let `` and `sizes` choose, and the browser picks the appropriate file for the device. Always set width and height, or an aspect-ratio in CSS. Without them the browser cannot reserve space, and the layout shifts as each image loads — the exact thing the Cumulative Layout Shift metric punishes. Then defer the ones below the fold with `loading="lazy"`, and give the hero the opposite treatment: `fetchpriority="high"` and a preload hint so it starts as early as possible. Those two attributes alone move the largest-contentful-paint number meaningfully.

title: Avoiding memory leaks in single-page apps
excerpt: Listeners, timers, subscriptions and closures. Leaks in a SPA accumulate instead of resetting.
content:
A server-rendered page throws its memory away on navigation. A single-page app does not, so anything you forget to clean up keeps accumulating for the whole session, and the tab slows to a crawl an hour in.

The usual suspects are all things that outlive a component: a `window` event listener, a `setInterval`, a WebSocket subscription, an observer. Each one holds a reference to the closure that registered it, and through it to the component's data.

React's effect cleanup is the remedy, and it is not optional. Register in the effect, unregister in the returned function, and be sure the effect returns a cleanup whenever it starts anything persistent.

Fetch requests count too. An in-flight request resolved after unmount updates state that no longer exists and keeps the component alive in a closure. Aborting with an `AbortController` in the cleanup closes both holes at once.

title: API versioning strategies
excerpt: Version the contract on purpose, and give clients a migration path you can defend.
content:
Every API changes, and the only question is whether you break consumers when it does. Versioning is the mechanism that lets you add capability without an outage for existing clients.

The simplest approach is a URL prefix, `/api/v1/`, which is explicit, cacheable and easy to route. Header-based version negotiation keeps URLs stable but is harder to test and debug, since the version is invisible in a browser address bar.

Additive changes do not need a new version. New fields in a response, new optional parameters and new endpoints are safe if clients are expected to ignore what they do not understand. Write that expectation into your contract, and document it.

When a break is unavoidable, ship the new version alongside the old, publish a deprecation date, and monitor usage per version. Retiring a version no one is calling is easy; discovering a forgotten integration the hard way is not.

title: CI/CD for small teams
excerpt: One pipeline that lints, tests and builds on every push. Keep it fast or nobody trusts it.
content:
Continuous integration starts as a single job: on every push, install dependencies, lint, run the tests and build. That alone catches the majority of integration mistakes before they reach a shared branch.

Speed is the feature. A pipeline that takes twenty minutes gets bypassed, so cache the dependency install, run jobs in parallel where they are independent, and fail fast on lint before spending time on the full build.

For delivery, start with a scripted deploy that anyone can run and that a machine can run identically. Deploy on merge to main, keep the artefact that was tested, and make rollback a redeploy of the previous artefact rather than a rebuild.

Add gates as the team grows: required reviews, a preview environment per pull request, a smoke test against the deployed URL. Each addition should remove a class of mistake, and anything that does not can wait.

title: Staying current without burning out
excerpt: Depth beats novelty. Choose a few sources, build small things, and ignore the rest.
content:
The firehose of new frameworks is not a signal about what matters. Most of what ships each month is a variation on an idea that already exists, and trying to track all of it is a direct route to exhaustion.

Pick a small number of sources you trust and read them properly instead of skimming everything. One good newsletter, one or two blogs, and the release notes of the tools you actually use will cover more ground than a hundred tabs.

Learning that sticks is built, not read. Recreate a small version of the thing you are curious about, in an afternoon, and you will understand it far better than a tutorial series would give you.

Finally, invest in the durable layer: HTTP, data structures, the browser platform, debugging, reading unfamiliar code. Those skills transfer across every framework you will ever be asked to learn, and they are the ones that make the new thing cheap.
